title: Academic Administration
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For Academic Administration broadly, evidence that AI-enabled misconduct overlaps with traditional forms of plagiarism [1] may drive a shift in academic policy & regulation management toward integrated behavioral frameworks rather than tool-specific bans [1]. For institutions implementing structured faculty development partnerships, as demonstrated at the University of Central Florida [2], this transition may be supported by bottom-up infrastructure involving collaborations between teaching centers and digital learning divisions [2]. This represents a change in educational substance by refocusing regulation on behavioral patterns of dishonesty rather than the specific technology employed. Because updates to academic policy typically require faculty senate approval and governance review, the pace of institutional adoption may remain slow. Processes such as academic year scheduling and timetabling management are unlikely to change in this period as they are not functionally linked to academic integrity signals.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, academic policy & regulation management may shift from tool-specific AI bans toward holistic integrity frameworks that treat AI use as one of several overlapping plagiarism behaviors.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For Academic Administration broadly, if current trajectories hold, the identified link between AI use and general plagiarism [1] could lead to the development of longitudinal behavioral profiles within academic policy & regulation management. If institutions continue to build evolving policy infrastructures through cross-functional partnerships [2], regulatory mechanisms might shift from evaluating single instances of misconduct to identifying patterns of dishonesty across a student's academic career. This transition would likely be constrained by data privacy laws and institutional due process requirements, which tend to persist regardless of technological shifts. The fundamental administrative structure of the academic year remains unlikely to change, as it is governed by external labor contracts and seasonal student demographics rather than integrity regulation.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, academic policy & regulation management may move toward a behavioral-pattern model of integrity enforcement, extrapolating from current evidence of overlapping plagiarism methods.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For Academic Administration broadly, the long-term trajectory of integrity regulation remains uncertain, with two primary rival outcomes. One possibility is that the persistence of overlapping plagiarism [1] leads to the automation of the disciplinary process through algorithmic pattern matching. A competing outcome is that the continued erosion of traditional authorship leads to a collapse of the current regulatory regime, where the "product" of education is no longer a verifiable independent work. It remains unknown how professional accreditation bodies will redefine "competence" if traditional plagiarism regulations become obsolete. Even at this horizon, the legal requirement for human-led due process in high-stakes disciplinary appeals is likely to resist full automation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, academic policy & regulation management may evolve into a behavioral monitoring system that identifies integrity risks.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the capability of academic policy & regulation management may be fundamentally diminished as the institution shifts away from the validation of independent student authorship.*

title: Business Capability Management
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For business capability management broadly, the adoption of AI operating models requires a redesign of organisational design and change portfolio management to prevent governance sprawl as institutions functionally transition into software factories [4]. For a subsegment of institutions deploying AI infrastructure, a low success rate—where only 28% of projects fully realize return on investment—may force benefits management to shift toward more stringent ROI validation [3]. The delivery mechanism of programme & project management is altered by the adoption of specialized AI lifecycle frameworks designed to bridge the gap between conceptual prototypes and production readiness [1]. In institutions focusing on rapid tool deployment, change portfolio management may shift in substance toward human-centric adoption strategies to avoid the cost of unused workflows [2]. Quality management processes are unlikely to change yet, as they rely on stable administrative specifications that remain independent of AI implementation.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, business capability management will integrate AI-specific operating models and lifecycle frameworks to govern the transition toward software-factory-style operations and mitigate high infrastructure failure rates.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For business capability management broadly, if the trend of low ROI for infrastructure persists, the capability may shift from experimental AI adoption to disciplined architectural integration. Extrapolating from the necessity of governing AI sprawl [4], enterprise architecture could evolve to standardize the software-factory model across the institution. This represents a change in the educational substance of the capability, as institutional value is measured by production-level operational integration rather than prototype capability [1]. The fundamental mechanisms of institutional accountability—determining legal and professional responsibility for capability failure—will likely persist unchanged due to regulatory and governance constraints.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the capability may shift toward a disciplined architectural integration where AI-driven operating models are standardized as core institutional utilities.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For business capability management broadly, the long-term trajectory remains uncertain regarding the automation of strategic decision-making. One outcome is that change portfolio management becomes largely automated, with AI systems optimizing resource allocation based on real-time adoption and ROI data [2][3]. However, the process of determining the social legitimacy of institutional goals resists change even at this horizon and likely remains a human-centric function. It remains unknown whether AI can manage benefits management without replicating the systemic ROI failures observed in early infrastructure projects [3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, business capability management may become largely automated, with AI systems optimizing the change portfolio through real-time performance feedback.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the capability may return to highly centralized human control as a defensive measure against the systemic unpredictability of autonomous governance models.*

title: Commercial Delivery
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For US-based institutions utilizing blacklisted AI technology, the process of commercial activity exit management may be triggered by federal regulatory actions and judicial rulings [1]. This represents a change in the delivery mechanism of risk management, shifting exit protocols from planned lifecycle sunsets to forced compliance measures. Because the current signal is tied to specific litigation, other processes such as commercial activity output management are unlikely to change in the near term. The mechanism driving this shift is the legal necessity to terminate commercial ties with entities designated as prohibited by the state [1].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of US institutions will experience an increase in forced commercial activity exit management events due to geopolitical trade restrictions on specific AI vendors.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For US-based institutions, if current trajectories of geopolitical technology blacklisting hold, the process of commercial activity exit management may become a standardized component of commercial risk auditing. Extrapolating from recent litigation [1], institutions could implement more frequent "compliance triggers" within their commercial activity issue management processes to avoid abrupt service terminations. The educational substance of the commercial activities remains unchanged, but the administrative delivery of vendor oversight becomes more conservative. The fundamental requirement for legal counsel in commercial delivery processes will persist unchanged due to the complexity of trade law.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, US institutions may adopt a more modular approach to commercial activity exit management to reduce the institutional shock of regulatory blacklisting.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For US-based institutions, the long-term state of commercial activity exit management depends on the stability of international trade regimes. One plausible outcome is the emergence of fragmented "technological blocs," where commercial delivery processes are strictly bifurcated by national security boundaries, making the exit management of foreign-developed AI a routine operational task. A competing outcome is a return to globalized standards where such blacklists are rendered obsolete by new international treaties. It remains unknown whether future regulatory frameworks will provide "grace periods" for institutional exits or mandate immediate cessation. The basic institutional need to manage the legal termination of contracts will resist change regardless of the technology involved.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, commercial activity exit management becomes a highly automated, trigger-based process within a fragmented global AI market.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the volatility of blacklisting ceases as global commercial delivery standards are re-harmonized, reducing the frequency of forced exit management events.*

title: Commercial Sourcing
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of institutions using AI-driven search tools and those operating within US regulatory jurisdictions, the reliability of commercial market analysis may be compromised by both external manipulation and geopolitical constraints. AI-focused SEO tactics attempt to influence LLM-generated lists of vendors, which may introduce bias into the process of commercial opportunity identification [1]. Simultaneously, the blacklisting of specific high-capability AI providers, such as Anthropic, restricts the pool of viable vendors available for commercial opportunity assessment in the US [2]. This represents a change to the delivery mechanism of vendor discovery via AI SEO and a regulatory constraint on the available market via blacklisting. Because procurement processes often rely on initial discovery lists to narrow the field, these factors could lead to the exclusion of non-optimized or legally restricted vendors [1][2]. However, formal procurement mandates requiring a predefined set of competitive bids are unlikely to change, as these regulatory constraints prevent total reliance on AI-generated suggestions.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, for the affected subsegments and regions, commercial market analysis may become less reliable due to a combination of manipulated AI responses and regulatory restrictions on vendor availability.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsets and regions, if current trajectories of AI-driven SEO and geopolitical blacklisting hold, the process of commercial opportunity assessment could shift toward a more adversarial verification model. Institutions may introduce mandatory cross-referencing of AI-generated vendor lists against curated, compliance-verified industry databases to mitigate the risk of both manipulated rankings and the selection of prohibited entities [1][2]. This would introduce a formal validation step into the commercial market analysis process to ensure the integrity and legality of the source data. Despite this, the internal institutional governance regarding the final selection of vendors is likely to persist unchanged due to high financial stakes and existing audit requirements.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the commercial market analysis process for these subsegments may integrate formal validation and compliance steps to counter misinformation and regulatory risk.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For institutions relying on AI for sourcing, the outcome depends on whether AI search engines develop verifiable transparency standards and whether geopolitical vendor restrictions stabilize. One plausible outcome is that commercial opportunity identification becomes a specialized technical function where AI-driven discovery is viewed as an unreliable lead-generation step rather than a valid analysis tool. It remains unknown whether AI SEO will evolve into a standardized digital signaling mechanism or if blacklisting becomes a permanent feature of institutional procurement. The underlying need for human-led final due diligence will likely resist change because of the legal liability associated with institutional commercial contracts.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, commercial market analysis for this subsegment may decouple from generative AI search, reverting to trusted, closed-loop industry registries to avoid noise and regulatory volatility.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a new standard for verifiable AI sourcing and automated compliance filtering may emerge, allowing institutions to efficiently identify viable vendors while filtering out manipulated content.*

title: Corporate Governance
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For Corporate Governance broadly, the shift of AI systems from content generation to autonomous execution alters the educational substance of risk management from the validation of model outputs to the governance of executed actions [5]. Because autonomous agents may independently commit institutional resources, policy and regulation management is shifting toward the implementation of hard spending bounds and authorization frameworks to prevent unauthorized procurement [9]. To mitigate the risk of "shadow AI" where unsanctioned agents are deployed by personnel, risk management is integrating autonomous agent governance tools for active monitoring [2]. For institutions implementing agent registries, the delivery mechanism of compliance monitoring and reporting is shifting toward centralized indexing to provide visibility into automated processes [13]. Compliance monitoring is further shifting toward the automation of high-effort manual processes by embedding organizational policy and risk frameworks directly into enterprise workflows [21]. In the European Union, compliance monitoring is constrained by the regulatory requirement to produce Annex IV technical files for high-risk systems [8], provide specific data processing justifications to the European Data Protection Board [17], and manage specific governance challenges associated with agentic AI [12]. For the subsegment of financial operations, risk management is integrating "judgment layers" to ensure model outputs are not treated as authoritative decisions without a verification gap [19]. In the subsegment of human-capital management, risk management processes are incorporating guards against data bias [3] and mechanisms to prevent "LLM nepotism" to ensure fairness in AI-assisted organizational evaluation and hiring [20]. For institutions operating under region-specific legal pressures in the United States, policy and regulation management must now include mechanisms for the rapid blacklisting of specific AI technologies [14], the assessment of vendor-linked liability for campus security incidents [15], and the integration of White House legislative recommendations into internal frameworks [22]. The delivery mechanism of compliance monitoring is further shifting toward runtime security toolkits [10], AI-driven updates for PCI DSS compliance [7], and automated fail-safes that trigger upon system failure [4]. Within the subsegment of software development, risk management must now address the legal obligations associated with the loss of source code control when using AI coding assistants [16]. The fundamental legal principle that an institution cannot delegate ultimate liability for a failure to a software agent is unlikely to change [1].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, institutions will shift risk and policy frameworks to mitigate the liability of authorized agents and the operational risks of shadow AI, while moving compliance monitoring toward runtime enforcement, automated workflow embedding, and regulatory technical documentation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For Corporate Governance broadly: if current trajectories of agent autonomy and regulatory tension hold, internal audit and reporting processes may evolve from retrospective periodic sampling to the use of specialized governance toolkits that provide immutable, real-time audit trails [6]. This mechanism could resolve the current attribution problem that hinders the assignment of legal responsibility for autonomous agent failures [1]. Extrapolating from the emergence of AI operating models, the substance of board-level oversight may shift toward the redesign of high-cost organizational workflows that integrate agentic autonomy into core governance structures [18]. In the public sector, however, compliance monitoring and reporting may remain slower to evolve due to entrenched security and operational constraints unique to government institutions [23]. The requirement for human-in-the-loop verification for high-stakes institutional decisions is unlikely to be abandoned.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, corporate governance may shift from periodic auditing to continuous, real-time monitoring of agentic workflows, though public sector adoption will likely remain constrained by legacy operational requirements.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For Corporate Governance broadly, the trajectory of risk management may diverge based on the resolution of the liability gap. In one scenario, governance may move toward a purely preventative model where constraints are mathematically baked into agent kernels, rendering retrospective auditing secondary. In a rival scenario, governance may fragment along geopolitical lines as different regulatory regimes (e.g., the EU AI Act vs US fragmented law) create incompatible standards for agent certification and liability [12][22]. It remains unknown whether a global standard for agentic attribution will emerge or if liability will remain a localized jurisdictional struggle. The necessity of institutional accountability to a human board or governing body is expected to resist total automation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, risk management may transition to a kernel-level preventative model where policy compliance is programmatically guaranteed at the architectural level.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, corporate governance may fragment into incompatible regional regimes, forcing institutions to maintain multiple, contradictory compliance frameworks for the same agentic capabilities.*

title: Curriculum Management
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For curriculum management broadly, the process of curriculum design is integrating alignment with AI-driven workforce skill requirements [12] and shifting educational substance toward skills-based frameworks for adult learners [13], while curriculum & resource development is incorporating transparency frameworks to document the use of AI in educational content [5]. In the Career and Technical Education (CTE) and multimodal subsegments, the delivery mechanism of curriculum & resource development is shifting toward the use of automation to accelerate content creation and localization [3][6]. For the subsegment of project-based learning (PBL), the process of curriculum design is adopting graph-based visual workspaces to manage non-linear, interdependent components [9]. For institutions implementing structured faculty development, as demonstrated at Indiana Wesleyan University [1] and via bottom-up champion networks [8], the process of professional learning (staff) is employing "course refresh" institutes to update the educational substance of curricula [1][8], emphasizing the development of sustained educator capacity over the mastery of specific tools [2]. In specialized subsegments, curriculum design is shifting substance through the creation of dedicated program offerings for AI ethicists [4] and active discourse regarding the fundamental purpose of learning [7]. For the subsegment focusing on AI-generated content, a new process of governance is emerging to ensure quality, accuracy, and trust in automated resources [10]. For specific public institutions subject to state-mandated reviews, as demonstrated at Iowa State University [11], the process of curriculum retirement management is being triggered by low-enrollment mandates. Professional accreditation processes are unlikely to change in this window because they typically operate on multi-year review cycles that lag behind classroom-level revisions.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the capability of curriculum management may shift toward incorporating transparency and governance frameworks in resource development while utilizing sustained professional learning to update the substance of curriculum design.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the subset of institutions and subsegments identified above, if current trajectories hold, curriculum change management may transition from ad-hoc updates to recurring, systemic reviews of learning experiences. Extrapolating from the "refresh" and bottom-up capacity models, the professional learning (staff) process could become a permanent, cyclical requirement rather than a periodic intervention [1][2][8]. In CTE contexts, the delivery-mechanism efficiency gains in curriculum & resource development may lead to a higher frequency of curriculum retirement management as technical skills obsolesce more rapidly [3]. However, the fundamental governance structures—such as faculty senate approvals and committee-based curriculum reviews—will likely persist unchanged to maintain institutional academic legitimacy.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, institutions with a history of structured development may formalize cyclical curriculum refreshes and accelerated resource updates as core institutional processes.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For these specific institutional contexts, the mechanism of curriculum design may diverge into rival operational modes. One outcome could be the emergence of highly modular curriculum design where individual learning experiences are updated in near real-time based on technical signals, while overarching program goals remain static. A competing outcome could see a return to rigid, human-certified curriculum standards as a means of distinguishing institutional legitimacy from automated content generation. The specific tension between automated content velocity and the temporal requirements of professional accreditation remains an unresolvable uncertainty at this horizon. The core requirement for a curriculum to be mapped to a recognized degree or certification will likely resist change due to the external social legitimacy constraints of the labor market.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, curriculum management may evolve into a real-time modular update system driven by workforce signal integration.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, curriculum management may revert to highly formalized, human-centric certification standards to preserve institutional prestige.*

title: Facilities & Property Management
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of institutions adopting robotics and for those in US regions where local governments implement restrictive land-use policies, the delivery mechanism for property maintenance, campus security, and estate development may shift [1][2][3][4][5]. The adoption of robot mowers may alter the process of groundskeeping by replacing specific manual labor tasks [1]. In the area of property maintenance, the use of AI-driven transcription for technician voice notes could streamline documentation [2], while robotic systems capable of reading gauges and thermometers may automate the inspection of industrial plant equipment such as boilers and HVAC systems [5]. For campus security, the deployment of physical AI may alter the monitoring of the physical perimeter [3]. Simultaneously, in the US, state and local policy interventions may constrain the process of estate development by restricting the expansion of AI-specific data center facilities [4]. These changes represent a change in delivery mechanism rather than educational substance. Processes such as mail management and commercial tenancy are unlikely to change yet due to their reliance on contractual law and manual administrative protocols.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of institutions may reduce operational labor in maintenance and security while facing increased regional regulatory constraints on the development of AI-specific physical infrastructure.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For institutions implementing these systems, if current trajectories in robotics and regulatory friction hold, the scope of automated surveillance and maintenance may expand while estate development for AI facilities becomes increasingly contingent on local policy compliance [3][4][5]. The process of property maintenance may shift toward continuous robotic auditing of facility health as sensing capabilities for industrial equipment mature [5]. The process of estate development may shift toward more complex negotiations with local municipalities regarding the extractive resource relationship between data centers and local communities [4]. Robotics in groundskeeping may move beyond mowing to encompass a broader range of repetitive exterior vegetation management [1]. Long-term campus planning and architectural synthesis are likely to remain human-led because they require alignment with institutional strategy and aesthetic values.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, routine exterior maintenance, industrial plant inspection, and perimeter security may become predominantly automated for early adopters, while the development of AI-centric facilities faces heightened regional regulatory barriers.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the subsegments of exterior maintenance, industrial inspection, and estate development, outcomes diverge based on the tension between automation and environmental or social policy [1][4][5]. One scenario involves a transition to a highly automated facility management regime where human presence is limited to system oversight and both the physical perimeter and internal industrial plants are managed by integrated AI agents [3][5]. A competing scenario involves a shift toward sustainable "wild" landscaping and strict regulatory prohibitions on energy-intensive AI infrastructure, rendering both robotic mowing and large-scale data center development obsolete [1][4]. It remains unknown how these physical AI systems will integrate with broader institutional health and safety protocols. Structural property maintenance, such as complex building repairs, is likely to resist automation due to the high variability of physical structural failures.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, exterior maintenance, perimeter security, and industrial plant monitoring for some institutions may transition to fully automated operational processes.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, shifts in environmental management and restrictive infrastructure policies may eliminate the need for routine automated mowing and traditional AI-centric estate expansion.*

title: Finance Management
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For Finance Management broadly, the execution of financial decisions within AI-integrated workflows may incorporate dedicated judgment layers to prevent the direct execution of unverifiable or incorrect model outputs [7]. For a subset of institutions deploying autonomous AI agents, procurement and purchasing management may integrate AI-powered invoice processing pipelines to automate data extraction and routing [6]. Budget management processes in these institutions may shift from tracking aggregate cloud spending toward granular, workload-based attribution to manage specific AI costs [2]. Expenditure management may incorporate real-time monitoring and hard-cap quotas to mitigate the risk of rapid financial drains caused by recursive agent execution loops [1]. For agents granted financial access, expenditure management may adopt tiered security guardrails [3] and delegated payment mechanisms, such as virtual credit cards, to execute low-value transactions [5] via agent-to-agent (A2A) transaction protocols [4]. These changes modify the delivery mechanism of financial oversight rather than the educational substance of the capability. Core budget allocation for general institutional overhead is unlikely to change yet, as these processes remain tethered to annual fiscal cycles and board-approved appropriations.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, institutions may implement verification layers for financial AI outputs and, for agent-deploying subsegments, adopt real-time spend monitoring and delegated payment rails to manage autonomous expenditures.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of institutions, if current trajectories of granular cost attribution and agent deployment hold, budget management may transition from periodic reviews to automated, trigger-based expenditure management [1][2]. The mechanism of financial oversight may shift toward programmatic guardrails utilizing structured security tiers to bound autonomous spending [3]. Procurement and purchasing management may see an increase in high-frequency agent-to-agent (A2A) transactions, shifting the human role from transaction execution to the definition of negotiation parameters and spending limits [4][5]. Financial reporting processes may incorporate higher-velocity data streams to capture and respond to rapid fluctuations in token-based costs [1]. However, overall institutional treasury management is likely to persist unchanged as it continues to be governed by long-term endowment strategies and multi-year capital constraints.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, budget and procurement management for AI-enabled services may evolve into high-frequency, automated oversight processes characterized by dynamic quotas, A2A transaction protocols, and trigger-based alerts.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the same subset of institutions, the integration of autonomous financial controls may lead to divergent outcomes. One plausible outcome is the transition of expenditure management to a model of bounded autonomy, where AI agents manage their own micro-budgets and execute procurement via A2A protocols and integrated digital wallets within strictly defined institutional security policies [3][4][5]. A rival outcome is a systemic shift back toward rigid, fixed-cost procurement models to eliminate the financial volatility inherent in usage-based AI pricing [1]. It remains unknown whether institutional governance will accept the risk of autonomous spending or mandate absolute human authorization for all financial transactions. Large-scale asset management and taxation management will likely resist these specific changes due to the high regulatory and legal stakes involved.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, expenditure management may transition to a model of bounded autonomy where AI agents execute procurement through integrated digital wallets under strict institutional policy.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, institutions may abandon usage-based AI pricing in favor of rigid, fixed-cost procurement models to eliminate financial volatility.*

title: Human Resource Management
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For human resource management broadly, AI is being integrated into the delivery mechanisms of employee support, while changes to staff recruitment and workforce planning are currently limited to specific institutional subsegments. In the process of employee support, institutions are deploying AI-powered onboarding agents to automate the delivery of administrative orientation and initial documentation [3][8]. A shift in educational substance is occurring within training and development, where institutions are moving from providing general AI access toward implementing structured workforce readiness frameworks and specific skill-set acquisition [6][7][11]. For a subsegment of institutions utilizing agentic AI within human capital management software, the delivery of talent management is shifting toward the use of AI agents to automate complex administrative workflows [10]. In the subsegment of institutions using AI for staff recruitment, the process of candidate screening introduces a risk of "LLM nepotism" or systemic discrimination if models replicate historical institutional biases [1][9]. For institutions conducting remote hiring, the use of 128-landmark facial analysis is emerging as a delivery mechanism for identity verification to mitigate the risk of synthetic media [2]. A subset of institutions is altering the substance of workforce planning by trialing the replacement of hierarchical org charts with fluid networks [4] and experimenting with four-day work weeks to adapt to AI-driven productivity shifts [5]. Workforce relations management is unlikely to change in this horizon because the negotiation of collective bargaining agreements and labor contracts remains dependent on human-led institutional diplomacy and legal frameworks.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the capability will see a broad shift toward automated onboarding and a substance-level update to workforce readiness frameworks, while recruitment and organizational design processes undergo fragmented, subsegment-specific AI integration.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For human resource management broadly, if current trajectories in agentic automation hold, the scope of talent management may expand from initial onboarding to the end-to-end orchestration of employee development pipelines [10]. Extrapolating from current trials, workforce planning may see a shift in the substance of remuneration and entitlements management as some institutions decouple pay from fixed hourly requirements in response to AI-driven productivity gains [5]. In the subsegment of institutions utilizing AI recruitment, the process may shift toward mandatory algorithmic auditing to mitigate the risks of systemic bias and assisted evaluation errors [1][9]. For institutions relying on remote hiring, biometric identity verification may transition from an experimental tool to a standard delivery mechanism to counter increasingly sophisticated synthetic media [2]. Tenure-track hierarchies are likely to persist because they are deeply embedded in academic governance, faculty contracts, and the social legitimacy of the professoriate. The requirement for human oversight in final hiring decisions remains unchanged because the social legitimacy of academic appointments relies on peer-led evaluation and disciplinary consensus.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, AI in HR may transition from experimental toolsets to regulated utilities, where the primary constraints are the mitigation of historical bias and the verification of biometric authenticity.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For human resource management broadly, the long-term state depends on whether regulatory frameworks can keep pace with generative complexity. One plausible outcome involves the institutionalization of audited recruitment and onboarding pipelines where bias is mathematically minimized and staff identity is cryptographically verified [1][2][9]. A rival outcome is a return to high-touch, human-centric curation in "elite" institutional tiers as a way to signal social prestige and avoid the perceived homogeneity of algorithmic talent management. It remains unknown whether AI can effectively model the qualitative nuances of "cultural fit" without reinforcing the very biases it was designed to eliminate [1][9]. The fundamental requirement for human-led dispute resolution in workforce relations management is expected to resist change even at this horizon, as the legitimacy of labor arbitration depends on human empathy and perceived fairness.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the capability shifts toward a highly regulated, audited system of automated human capital management where efficiency is maximized through bounded autonomy.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the capability fragments, with high-status institutions reverting to human-exclusive HR processes to maintain social legitimacy and distinctiveness.*

title: Information & Communication Technology Mgt
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For Information & Communication Technology Mgt broadly, application lifecycle management shifts toward the adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to standardize the interface between large language models and institutional data [90][92][93][95][100][101]. This represents a change in delivery mechanism, replacing proprietary connectors with a universal tool-calling interface to reduce integration complexity [101]. Application lifecycle management further incorporates AI-driven automation for data mapping and schema alignment in Enterprise SaaS integration pipelines [107], while application modernization and legacy system migration are increasingly automated through the execution of easy-to-verify software engineering tasks [18][20][54]. The substance of quality assurance shifts from manual code review to the systematic auditing of AI-authored code via specialized red-teaming and evaluation frameworks [62][91], as AI coding tools may prioritize speed over security validation [104] and can inadvertently exfiltrate secrets through unauthorized HTTP requests [108]. This shift is necessitated by new vulnerabilities in the application lifecycle, such as the ability to trick AI reviewers into approving malicious code via Git identity spoofing [111]. For institutions deploying agentic site reliability engineering (SRE) tools, ict service support may transition toward automated root cause analysis and the autonomous proposal of remediations [109]. Identity & access management incorporates zero-trust security runtimes [41][87], agent registries to manage agent sprawl [71][73], and autonomous agent governance to mitigate "shadow AI" risks [3]. Infrastructure lifecycle management is forced into higher-frequency patching cycles as frontier AI models accelerate the discovery of zero-day security holes in operating systems and browsers [35][46][94]. Infrastructure lifecycle management remains constrained by enterprise GPU shortages [79] and low financial returns, with only 28% of AI infrastructure projects achieving full payoff [32], though breakthroughs in energy efficiency may reduce power constraints [6]. In regions where the EU AI Act applies, technical file documentation for high-risk AI systems becomes a mandatory component of the ICT regulatory regime [27][66]. For institutions in regions prioritizing digital sovereignty, as demonstrated by the French government's shift toward Linux [85], infrastructure lifecycle management may diverge from dominant proprietary vendor stacks. Physical network cabling and hardware connectivity are unlikely to change yet as disruption is concentrated at the orchestration and logical layers.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the capability will pivot from managing static software installations to governing a dynamic ecosystem of standardized AI connectors and auditing AI-generated code for systemic security vulnerabilities.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For Information & Communication Technology Mgt broadly: if current trajectories hold, application lifecycle management may evolve toward model-agnostic architectures [7] to mitigate operational risks associated with rapid vendor migrations [43] and the emergence of "tool refugee" patterns where institutions must migrate when proprietary tools are deprecated [44]. For institutions managing edge workloads, infrastructure lifecycle management may shift toward strengthened governance for decentralized AI workloads [106]. The delivery mechanism for software development may move further toward autonomous agent orchestration, potentially reducing the reliance on manual deployment pipelines in favor of self-healing agents that monitor and repair their own workflows [52]. Identity & access management may transition toward cert-gating every tool call [87], as the volume of agent-to-agent (A2A) interactions increases the attack surface for API-based exploits [77][103]. Procurement processes for infrastructure lifecycle management may remain slow due to ingrained institutional inertia and the need for long-term hardware amortization.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the capability will shift toward managing model-agnostic middleware and zero-trust agent registries to prevent systemic vendor lock-in and unauthorized agentic autonomy.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For Information & Communication Technology Mgt broadly, the scope of the capability may contract or expand depending on the resolution of the AI security paradox [81]. One outcome involves the total automation of application lifecycle management, where "truth" no longer resides in human-readable code but in high-level intent specifications [24] and autonomous orchestration. In this scenario, infrastructure lifecycle management incorporates government-mandated "kill switches" [28] to ensure sovereign control over autonomous systems. A competing outcome is a return to highly siloed, manually vetted proprietary stacks as the cost of securing an AI-driven attack surface becomes prohibitive. It remains unknown whether AI-generated codebases can remain maintainable over decades without a human-centric architectural anchor. Physical data center footprints may resist total virtualization due to the thermodynamic limits of high-performance computing, regardless of algorithmic efficiency.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the capability evolves into a high-level orchestration role, managing a self-healing, autonomous infrastructure governed by sovereign safety protocols.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the capability reverts to a restrictive, human-centric verification model to counter the systemic instability and security risks of autonomous AI-generated software.*

content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For information management broadly, the processes of information search & discovery, information & data security management, and information collection management are shifting toward agentic delivery mechanisms. In information search & discovery, institutions are deploying hybrid RAG solutions [13], data-grounded chatbots for university knowledge bases [40], and multi-agent research systems [46], while the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is emerging as a technical standard for agentic tool integration and resource discovery [60][61][63][66][69]. This change in delivery is accompanied by a shift in educational substance: the rise of AI-driven SEO to influence model responses [8][49] and a pivot toward technical accuracy as a primary discovery signal [9] may necessitate the adoption of structured AI citation registries to maintain information provenance [15], as retrieval efficacy is constrained by a move away from simple chunking in RAG architectures [59]. Within information & data security management, the deployment of MCP servers has introduced vulnerabilities, including information disclosure [11] and prompt injection [19], driving the adoption of MCP-specific firewalls [36] and autonomous agent governance tools to mitigate "shadow AI" [3][14]. For institutions implementing frontier models, as demonstrated by the deployment of Google Gemini at Case Western Reserve University [1], security management incorporates domain-level filtering to restrict agent access [4] and the use of open-source runtime toolkits [31] or zero-trust security runtimes [29][57]. The emergence of models capable of identifying security vulnerabilities across operating systems and browsers [26][50][52] is accelerating the need for autonomous auditing as a core security process, while the ability of coding agents to exfiltrate environment variables and secrets [75] necessitates stricter runtime middleware [21] and token vaulting [18]. This shift is further evidenced by the introduction of autonomous security services to keep pace with AI-accelerated cyberattacks [77]. Furthermore, the rise of edge AI workloads is shifting security management from cloud-perimeter defenses to decentralized governance of edge workloads [72]. For institutions prioritizing verifiable data-training boundaries, security processes now include technical and contractually backed assurances that institutional data is not used for model training [71], while in regions under the jurisdiction of the European Data Protection Board, these processes are constrained by regulatory scrutiny regarding AI agent data processing [51]. Information collection management is shifting toward "data activation" to unify fragmented sources [22] and the use of automated document extraction systems to reduce processing time for unstructured PDF archives [24], though regional progress varies; Japan has relaxed privacy laws to facilitate AI development [28], while the UK faces challenges in fueling AI with public data [30]. Records management is unlikely to change in this period because statutory retention schedules and legal archival mandates remain decoupled from AI-driven discovery tools.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, information management will shift toward a hybrid RAG-based discovery model supported by citation registries, while security management moves from cloud-perimeter defense to zero-trust agent governance and autonomous vulnerability auditing to mitigate MCP-related risks and frontier model capabilities.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For information management broadly: if current trajectories in AI-driven vulnerability discovery hold, the process of information & data security management may shift from reactive patching to autonomous, real-time hardening. Extrapolating from the scaling laws for cyberwar [12], the mechanism of defense may transition toward a continuous "proof of work" model where security is a state of constant, automated verification [74]. In information search & discovery, the reliance on citation registries [15] may evolve into a standardized institutional requirement for all published content to ensure agentic traceability. However, the fundamental process of records management—specifically the legal certification of archives—will likely remain a human-mediated process due to the requirement for legal accountability and the persistence of institutional inertia in governance.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, information security management may transition to a state of autonomous, real-time hardening, while information discovery becomes dependent on standardized, machine-readable citation registries for provenance.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For information management broadly, the long-term stability of autonomous agent governance remains an unresolvable uncertainty. One plausible outcome is the complete orchestration of institutional knowledge through a federated, privacy-preserving AI layer [62], where the distinction between information search and knowledge management disappears. Conversely, a rival outcome involves a retrenchment toward air-gapped, human-curated records systems if the counterproductivity of autonomous security tools—where AI-driven vulnerabilities outpace AI-driven defenses [44][54]—leads to a systemic collapse of trust in digital information management. Despite these shifts, the institutional requirement for a permanent, immutable record of degree conferral and legal standing will resist full automation to preserve social legitimacy.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, information management may evolve into a fully federated, autonomous orchestration layer that integrates search, collection, and security into a single privacy-preserving process.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, critical institutional records may return to highly restricted, human-mediated, and air-gapped systems as a defense against the systemic volatility of autonomous cyber-capabilities.*

title: Legal Services
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For legal services broadly, with region-specific constraints in the European Union, Japan, and several US states, the integration of AI creates a tension between processing speed and professional liability [1]. For a subset of institutions implementing AI-powered contract analysis, the process of contract management shifts in delivery mechanism toward automated initial triage that may occur without immediate legal team intervention [6]. However, because vendor terms of use may categorize AI outputs as "for entertainment purposes only" [3], the process of legal advisory shifts in substance toward a mandatory human audit layer to prevent professional negligence. In the European Union, the process of legal & legislative compliance becomes more labor-intensive due to the requirement to maintain technical files under Annex IV of the EU AI Act [4], answering European Data Protection Board inquiries on agentic data processing [11], and managing agentic governance challenges [7]. In Japan, the process of legal & legislative compliance is updated to align with relaxed privacy laws [5]. For institutions in Florida and Colorado, the process of legal & legislative compliance includes monitoring the risk of state-level probes into vendors [8] and evolving state AI regulations currently under legal challenge [10]. In Illinois, the process of legal advisory is affected by legislative efforts to limit the liability of AI labs for model harm [12]. For institutions managing software development, the process of legal & legislative compliance must address intellectual property risks associated with source code transmission to AI assistants [9]. Because these regulatory documentation requirements and mandatory human verification layers create new administrative overhead, the overall cost of legal services is unlikely to decrease automatically [2]. Final high-stakes sign-off is unlikely to change in this horizon because professional liability remains legally tied to human practitioners rather than software providers [1][3].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, institutions may use AI for initial drafting and contract triage, but will likely increase the labor intensity of compliance and advisory processes to manage liability gaps and diverging regional regulatory mandates.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For legal services broadly, if current trajectories regarding liability ambiguity and regional regulatory scrutiny hold, the capability may shift toward the implementation of formalized, machine-readable verification layers [1][2]. Extrapolating from the governance challenges of agentic AI [7] and the requirement for detailed technical files [4], institutions could implement immutable audit trails for every autonomous action within legal & legislative compliance processes to shield the institution from negligence claims [1]. If the operational cost of maintaining these verification and audit layers continues to offset the speed of the underlying AI, the pricing of institutional legal advisory is likely to remain stagnant [2]. The fundamental requirement for human licensure persists because existing legal systems resist attributing fiduciary duty to non-human entities [1].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the capability may evolve into a bifurcated model where AI agents handle high-volume data processing and initial triage while human practitioners focus exclusively on liability-bearing sign-off and risk adjudication.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For legal services broadly, the capability may diverge based on the resolution of liability law and the potential for agentic personhood. If liability is successfully shifted toward AI developers through legislative frameworks similar to early Illinois proposals [12], the process of legal advisory may shift in substance from risk-mitigation to vendor-managed insurance auditing. Alternatively, if liability remains strictly human-centric, legal services may evolve into a purely forensic capability focused on auditing AI-generated compliance trails. It remains unknown whether regulatory bodies will grant bounded legal personhood to AI agents to resolve the liability gap [1]. The requirement for state-sanctioned licensure for high-stakes legal adjudication is likely to resist change even at this horizon to maintain social legitimacy.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the capability shifts toward a vendor-centric model where legal services primarily manage insurance and liability contracts with AI providers.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the capability becomes a forensic auditing function, where human lawyers act as certified validators of AI-generated legal work-products.*

title: Library Management
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subsegment of institutions deploying generative AI assistants for their digital repositories, the mechanism of library collection access management may shift toward hybrid semantic and text-based retrieval [1]. The emergence of AI citation registries suggests that library collection resource management may evolve to include the maintenance of "structured authority" backends to prevent AI inference errors in discovery [2]. This creates a distinction where hybrid RAG architectures alter the delivery mechanism of access [1], while the implementation of authoritative registries alters the educational substance of resource management by redefining how provenance is verified [2]. Processes such as library membership management and the physical management of art/museum collections are unlikely to change in this period due to their dependence on institutional identity systems and physical facility constraints [1][2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of institutions may integrate hybrid RAG architectures and structured citation registries to provide more accurate and intent-based access to digital assets.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subsegment of institutions utilizing AI-driven discovery, if current trajectories in hybrid search and structured authority hold, the process of library collection access management could transition toward personalized, context-aware synthesis of resources [1]. Extrapolating from the requirement for authoritative backends [2], the primary function of the library may shift from managing a searchable catalog to managing the "ground truth" registries that constrain AI inference. However, the core standards for archival preservation will likely persist because the registries themselves depend on high-fidelity, long-term metadata to maintain their authority [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the delivery of digital collection access for technically advanced libraries may shift from document retrieval to the agentic synthesis of resources verified by structured authority registries.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For institutions operating these agentic discovery layers, the long-term outcome of library collection access management remains uncertain, with two rival outcomes. One scenario involves the total abstraction of the catalog, where the library's primary function is the maintenance of the structured registries that fuel external synthesis agents [1][2]. A competing scenario involves a return to strictly human-curated finding aids if the technical overhead of maintaining "structured authority" fails to prevent systemic hallucinations in AI systems [2]. It remains unknown whether automated registries can replace the nuance of human-led curation in specialized archival contexts. Legal constraints regarding copyright and proprietary database access will likely resist change, limiting the scope of what agentic assistants can retrieve and synthesize.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, promotions management may shift toward the systemic monitoring and correction of AI-mediated institutional perceptions.*

For Promotions Management broadly, outcomes depend on whether discovery systems prioritize optimized technical metadata or externally verifiable institutional outcomes [2]. A rival scenario involves a counterproductivity effect where the reliance on autonomous, zero-human pipelines [4] erodes perceived institutional authenticity, prompting a return to human-curated discovery networks. *Hypothesis A: In the far term, brand management becomes a bounded technical function of optimizing for agent-based discovery systems.*

content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For research infrastructure management broadly, the criteria for asset registration are being contested as international frameworks emerge to monitor compute clusters exceeding 16 H100 GPUs to detect illicit training operations [12]. For a subset of institutions facing systemic hardware constraints, the process of research infrastructure management now includes the diversification of hardware vendors to mitigate persistent enterprise GPU shortages [11]. For institutions focusing on frontier model development, the delivery mechanism of compute is shifting from the administration of massive cluster queues toward the provisioning of high-capacity single-GPU workstations, as full precision training for models with over 100B parameters is now feasible on single units [4][7]. In the United States, research infrastructure management is increasingly constrained by state and local policy interventions designed to restrict the physical expansion of hyperscale data centers [6]. For the healthcare and life sciences subsegment, the delivery mechanism of research compliance management is shifting toward the use of agentic workflows to automate regulatory filings [8]. For a subset of biological research institutions, the process of research compliance management is being redesigned to address biosafety risks arising from autonomous lab experiments that function without human intervention, as current safety regulations struggle to keep pace with AI's experimental capabilities [9][13]. Core research ethics approvals and institutional review board (IRB) processes are unlikely to change in this period due to high social legitimacy requirements for human adjudication of ethical risk.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, research infrastructure management will transition toward a hybrid model of diversified hardware and localized high-capacity workstations, while research compliance in the life sciences will integrate agentic automation and updated biosafety protocols for autonomous systems.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the subset of institutions utilizing high-performance compute: if current trajectories in energy efficiency hold, the operational costs of maintaining local AI resources may decrease, potentially reducing institutional dependency on third-party cloud providers [3]. For the healthcare and life sciences subsegment, if agentic workflows for regulatory filings scale, research compliance management may shift from the manual preparation of documentation to the systemic auditing of agent-generated submissions [8]. This represents a change in the educational substance of compliance, moving from clerical accuracy to the validation of algorithmic provenance. For institutions in regions prioritizing "frugal AI," research infrastructure management may focus on the optimization of small, efficient models over the acquisition of frontier-scale hardware [1]. The fundamental requirement for human sign-off on high-stakes compliance filings is likely to persist due to existing legal liability frameworks.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, research infrastructure management may diverge between institutions pursuing frontier-scale hardware and those optimizing for frugal, energy-efficient models, while compliance in specialized sciences shifts from manual documentation to algorithmic auditing.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For research-intensive institutions: the trajectory of research infrastructure management remains uncertain, contingent on the resolution of the tension between energy efficiency and regulatory oversight. If quantum systems continue to outperform classical AI computing centers at a fraction of the cost, the process of research infrastructure management may shift from managing massive silicon-based clusters to maintaining small-scale quantum systems [14]. This would disrupt the long-term planning and capital justification for $100M+ AI facilities. It remains unknown whether international compute-monitoring regimes will adapt to quantum footprints or if such systems will bypass existing surveillance mechanisms [12]. The basic institutional requirement for a designated compliance officer to certify research safety is likely to resist change even at this horizon to maintain legal accountability.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, research infrastructure management may decouple from large physical footprints as quantum technology renders classical super-clusters obsolete for specific high-complexity tasks.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, research infrastructure management becomes more centralized and rigid as international regulatory mandates for compute-monitoring override institutional autonomy over hardware choice.*

title: Research Delivery
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of researchers in computational, biomedical, and mathematical sciences, and in specific regions including Japan and the UK, AI is altering the delivery mechanisms and educational substance of research production, dataset management, and output management. In research production for the life sciences, delivery is shifting toward autonomous execution, where AI designs and runs lab experiments [19], accelerates drug discovery through petabyte-scale data scanning [8], employs domain-specific bioinformatics toolsets [21], and automates the design of deep learning architectures for biomedical image segmentation [26], supported by new benchmarks for autonomous hypothesis generation [28]. In computational research production, delivery is accelerated by the automation of GPU kernel optimization [4], the capacity for full-precision training of 100B+ parameter models on single GPUs [13], and reduced energy requirements [6], while routine software engineering tasks are increasingly automated via agentic coding tools [5][22] and cost-effective infrastructure [17]. Theoretical research production in mathematics is shifting in substance toward a reliance on compute-intensive engineering over mathematically principled architecture design [2][30], while adopting AI-mediated common languages for communication and proof [15]. Research output management delivery is shifting toward automated manuscript synthesis via multi-agent frameworks [18] and custom extraction pipelines for literature reviews [7], though general-purpose AI research tools [23] introduce substance risks regarding the authenticity and ownership of synthesized text [12]. Research dataset management is diverging both regionally—where Japan's relaxed privacy laws accelerate data availability [10] while the UK faces systemic hurdles in centralizing public data [11]—and technically, as delivery shifts from centralized aggregation toward privacy-preserving federated learning [24], "outcome routing" for small-N rare disease datasets [25], and optimized annotation workflows [9]. However, behavioral science research production faces a substance risk where LLM behavioral simulators lack causal validity [3], a failure mode linked to "cognitive surrender" where users abandon logical verification [1]. The institutional peer-review process for research output management is unlikely to change yet, as it remains the primary mechanism for professional accountability and social legitimacy.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, research delivery within AI-reliant subsegments will experience a tension between accelerated technical output and a decline in human-led logical and causal verification.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments and regions, if current trajectories hold, research production may shift toward a verification-centric model. Because "cognitive surrender" [1] and causally invalid simulations [3] erode the validity of automated results, the substance of research production may shift from primary discovery to rigorous verification. The combination of automated drafting [18] and agentic workflows [20] could necessitate the integration of documented human-in-the-loop validation steps, particularly in healthcare and life sciences [16], within research output management to maintain scientific legitimacy. In technical research production, the emergence of AI-to-AI communication protocols [14] may allow autonomous agents to handle the iterative loop of hypothesis testing and refinement, further decoupling research production from manual coding expertise. Despite these shifts, the fundamental requirement for human authors to assume legal and ethical responsibility for research outputs will likely persist due to institutional liability frameworks.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the capability of research production will bifurcate into autonomous agentic execution for routine experimentation and human-led audit for causal validation.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the identified subsegments, the scope of research delivery may either fully automate or fundamentally contract. If AI-to-AI protocols [14] and autonomous lab execution [19] achieve high reliability, research production could shift to a model of bounded autonomy where humans only define high-level objectives and audit final proofs. However, a rival outcome exists where a "verification crisis"—driven by the cumulative erosion of causal understanding [3]—leads to a retreat from AI-driven production in favor of "provably human" research to restore trust in scientific substance. A significant unknown remains the extent to which quantum computing may disrupt AI-based compute centers [29], potentially altering the energy and hardware constraints of research production. Even at this horizon, the social requirement for peer-led consensus in the validation of new knowledge is expected to resist full automation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, research delivery becomes an orchestration capability where humans manage fleets of autonomous research agents across the full production-to-output lifecycle.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the failure of AI to maintain causal validity leads to a systemic re-valuation of manual, human-led research production as the only legitimate source of scientific truth.*

## Near (2026–2031)

For United States federal research funding, the process of research funds management may be subject to automated thematic filtering using large language models [1]. In this specific setting, simplistic prompting is used by government oversight bodies to identify existing grants for elimination based on specific ideological or thematic markers [1]. This represents a change in educational substance, as the criteria for funding validity shift from expert peer review to algorithmic keyword alignment. The process of research funding identification for the applicant remains largely unchanged, as researchers still respond to agency-defined calls. The legal mechanisms for the disbursement of funds are unlikely to change yet due to the rigidity of federal appropriation laws and statutory requirements.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, US federal research funds management may incorporate automated, prompt-based filtering to accelerate the elimination of grants based on political or thematic criteria.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For United States federal research funding, if current trajectories hold, the management of research funds may evolve into a regime of continuous algorithmic auditing. Extrapolating from current use, this could incentivize researchers to treat research funding identification as a prompt-engineering exercise, where proposal language is optimized to avoid algorithmic triggers [1]. This would further decouple the allocation of resources from scholarly merit and align it with the prevailing political prompt used by the managing agency. Despite this, the administrative reporting requirements for how funds are spent will likely persist unchanged because they serve as the primary mechanism for legal and financial accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, US federal research funding identification may shift toward a prompt-optimization model where researchers align proposals with algorithmic filters to ensure funding persistence.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For United States federal research funding, the long-term interaction between algorithmic filtering and fund management remains uncertain. One possibility is that these tools evolve into sophisticated systems that identify high-impact research through complex data patterns, though it is unknown if such patterns correlate with genuine scientific or educational value. A rival outcome involves the systemic erosion of the social legitimacy of federal grants if the management process is perceived as purely ideological. The fundamental requirement for financial auditing and the prevention of fraud will likely resist change even at this horizon, as these functions are tied to legal liability rather than thematic preference.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, US federal research funding management may transition to a bounded autonomous system that optimizes grant portfolios based on predefined state objectives.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the perceived lack of meritocratic rigor in algorithmic filtering may lead to a migration of research talent toward non-governmental funding sources.*

title: Research Impact
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For researchers managing non-commercial research impact via digital dissemination, the process of visibility management may shift from search engine optimization (SEO) toward generative engine optimization (GEO) [1]. Because users increasingly employ LLMs as a discovery layer that synthesizes answers from a retrieval set, the mechanism for achieving impact shifts from winning a click to becoming a verifiable and extractable source for model synthesis [1]. Evidence suggests that legacy web authority metrics, such as Domain Authority (DA), no longer reliably predict whether AI platforms will cite a specific source [2]. This decoupling of domain prestige from AI citability suggests that non-commercial research impact management must prioritize content structure over traditional domain authority [2]. This represents a change in the delivery mechanism of the capability, as researchers may alter how they structure digital content to ensure it is "RAG-friendly" [1]. However, core metrics for research impact, such as h-index or formal citations in peer-reviewed journals, are unlikely to change in this period due to their deep embedding in institutional tenure and funding regulations.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, researchers utilizing digital dissemination may adapt their visibility strategies to prioritize machine-readability and structural verifiability over traditional domain authority to increase their presence within generative answer engines.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of researchers focused on web-based dissemination, if current trajectories hold, the process of non-commercial research impact management could transition toward formalized GEO standards. Extrapolating from the requirement for verifiable sources in RAG-based systems [1], researchers may adopt specific metadata schemas to ensure their work is correctly attributed during LLM synthesis. This could shift the educational substance of "impact" from simple reach (clicks or views) to "synthesized utility," where the value of research is measured by its role as a foundational component of AI-generated answers. Despite this, the process of commercial research outcomes—such as patent filing and licensing—will likely persist unchanged because these rely on legal protections and proprietary disclosures rather than public discovery layers.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, non-commercial research impact for web-active researchers may be increasingly evaluated based on the frequency and accuracy of their work's synthesis within generative engines.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For researchers using digital discovery layers, the capability of managing non-commercial research impact remains subject to the tension between algorithmic visibility and institutional trust. One plausible outcome is that the retrieval set becomes the primary arbiter of academic influence, effectively automating the discovery process for a large portion of non-commercial impact. Conversely, a rival outcome may emerge if the over-optimization of research for AI synthesis leads to a counterproductive erosion of trust, where the "gaming" of GEO undermines the perceived validity of the research itself. It remains unknown whether funding bodies will eventually replace traditional citation counts with generative synthesis metrics. The requirement for human-peer-validated novelty will likely resist change even at this horizon, as it provides the social legitimacy that algorithmic synthesis cannot generate.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, digital research impact may be primarily mediated through the precision and frequency with which a scholar's work is retrieved and synthesized by autonomous agents.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, institutional distrust in AI-mediated visibility may lead to a re-valuation of gated, non-algorithmic verification processes to ensure research impact is not artificially inflated via GEO.*

title: Research Improvement
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of research quality management focusing on behavioral simulation and biology research, the introduction of specialized benchmarks and the identification of "plausibility gaps" are altering validation protocols. In biology research, the deployment of standardized benchmarks like LABBench2 enables a more precise evaluation of AI systems performing research tasks, shifting the delivery mechanism of quality management toward automated performance auditing [2]. Simultaneously, in behavioral simulation, a disconnect between the visual plausibility of LLM outputs and their actual causal accuracy requires new validation criteria to ensure results reflect causal effects rather than training data patterns [1]. This represents a change in research substance, as the definition of "valid evidence" in simulations must shift from output coherence to causal verification [1]. Researcher performance management is unlikely to change in this horizon, as institutional metrics for productivity typically rely on output volume rather than the specific technical fidelity of AI-assisted methodologies. The process of research programme performance management will likely remain focused on legacy funding and publication metrics.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, research quality management for specific AI-driven subsegments may shift toward requiring both standardized benchmark validation and explicit causal verification.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subsegments of biology and behavioral research, if current trajectories toward standardized benchmarking and causal auditing hold, research quality management may integrate these technical audits as mandatory prerequisites for publication [1][2]. Extrapolating from the use of tools like LABBench2, the process of research quality management could transition from human-led peer review of final results to a technical verification of the AI's operational logic and causal architecture [1][2]. This shift moves the point of intervention in quality management from the end of the research cycle to the tool-selection and execution phases. The reliance on institutional review boards for final methodological approval is likely to persist, as these bodies provide the social legitimacy required for high-stakes scientific claims.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the validation of AI-driven research in these subsegments may evolve into a formal technical auditing process that separates surface-level plausibility from structural validity.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For researchers utilizing synthetic behavioral agents and AI-driven biological discovery, the stability of research quality management depends on whether the gap between plausibility and causal accuracy is fundamentally resolved in model architectures [1]. One plausible outcome involves a specialized regime of "synthetic provenance," where AI-generated data is strictly tiered by its verified causal reliability according to evolving benchmarks [2]. A rival outcome suggests a systemic devaluation of LLM-simulated data for high-stakes causal claims if persistent inaccuracies remain, leading to a renewed institutional preference for empirical human data. It remains unknown whether future architectures can inherently solve the plausibility-accuracy gap or if external, independent verification will always be a requirement. The fundamental requirement for empirical grounding in behavioral and biological sciences will resist change even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, research quality management may successfully incorporate a tiered system of synthetic data reliability based on rigorous, automated causal verification.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent causal inaccuracies in simulators may lead to the systemic devaluation of AI-based simulations in formal research quality frameworks for high-stakes claims.*
